title: From the Cell to the Courtyard: Der Sozialist, the Twelve Articles, and the Bavarian Council Republic
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Karlsruhe, the shoe merchant's third son
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The schooling folded into this stop is dated only to the 1880s in the German article, which gives the Bismarck-Gymnasium without years; its coordinate, 49.0134 / 8.3949, is about 1.5 km from the birth pin used here.
stops.campa: In the capital of the Grand Duchy of Baden a third child is born to Hermann Landauer, shoe merchant, and Rosa Landauer, born Neuburger, a comfortable Jewish household whose roots run back into rural Swabia. The boy is registered Gustav. Karlsruhe is a residence city laid out in rays from a palace, orderly to the point of diagram, and he is put through the Bismarck-Gymnasium in the ordinary way: Latin, Greek, the German classics, the whole apparatus of a Baden bourgeois education. It is the only formal schooling he ever completes.
suggested_refs: The Bismarck-Gymnasium at Karlsruhe, his only formal schooling completed

stops.name: Heidelberg, the first matriculation
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day set to 01 to order the segment. Contradiction, not resolved: the English chronology places 1888 in Berlin, the German article puts Heidelberg first with Berlin from spring 1889 and Strasbourg around 1890. The German sequence is followed here, and the Heidelberg span is narrowed to 1888-1889 rather than the 1888-1891 one compilation gives, which would overlap the other two universities.
stops.campa: At eighteen he matriculates at the Ruprecht-Karls-Universität to read Germanistik, philosophy and history. Heidelberg is the oldest university in the German lands, a place of duelling corps and careful philology, and it holds him about a year. Berlin follows, then Straßburg: three universities in three years, none of them finished. He takes no degree here or anywhere afterward, and no salary from an institution of any kind, and he will do his reading for the next thirty years without a faculty behind him. Why he broke off is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The philosophical faculty of the Ruprecht-Karls-Universität, Heidelberg, winter semester 1888

stops.name: Berlin, the meeting with Fritz Mauthner
stops.date_confidence: Spring 1889 attested by the German article; month set to April and day to 01 to order the segment.
stops.campa: In the spring he comes to the Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität, and in Berlin he meets Fritz Mauthner, who is beginning the work that will become the Beiträge zu einer Kritik der Sprache. Mauthner holds that words do not reach the world, that every concept is a worn coin, that philosophy is at bottom a critique of its own vocabulary. Landauer takes this as a starting point rather than a defeat: if language cannot deliver reality, something else must, and he will spend fourteen years arguing that what it delivers is mysticism. The friendship lasts until his death.
suggested_refs: Fritz Mauthner, Beiträge zu einer Kritik der Sprache (1901-1902), whose manuscript Landauer later edited in prison

stops.name: Straßburg, the last matriculation
stops.date_confidence: Circa 1890-1891; the sources give no month, so month and day are set to 01. The Strasbourg period is the least documented of the three and is attested only as a span in compiled biographies.
stops.campa: He spends a stretch at the Kaiser-Wilhelms-Universität in Straßburg, the German university planted in annexed Alsace after 1871 to make the province German by lecture. It is his third and last matriculation. He does not finish it either. Berlin is pulling him back, and what pulls is not a faculty but a movement: the free stage, the workers' theatre, the independent socialists who think the Social Democratic Party has already made its peace with the Reich. He returns to the capital in 1891 without a degree and with no intention of getting one.
suggested_refs: The Kaiser-Wilhelms-Universität at Straßburg, founded 1872 in the annexed province

segments.name: Der Sozialist: The Paper, the Congress, the Cell

stops.name: Berlin, the Freie Volksbühne and Der Sozialist
stops.date_confidence: Volksbühne membership attested to April 1891; the editorial board of Der Sozialist and the Verein Unabhängiger Sozialisten date from February 1892 and are folded into this stop. Der Todesprediger appears in 1893. The editorial-office coordinate is approximate: the sources name the paper, not a street address.
stops.campa: He joins the Freie Volksbühne, the free people's stage, where workers pay a few pfennigs a month and see Ibsen and Hauptmann; then the Verein Unabhängiger Sozialisten; then, in February 1892, the editorial board of Der Sozialist. The paper is small, poor, permanently at law with the Prussian police, and it will be his organ for twenty-three years across three separate lives and deaths. In 1893 he publishes a philosophical novel, Der Todesprediger, whose hero preaches death and is argued out of it. He is twenty-two years old.
suggested_refs: Der Sozialist, first series, Berlin, from February 1892
Gustav Landauer, Der Todesprediger (1893)

stops.name: Zurich, the anarchists put out of the hall
stops.date_confidence: August 1893 attested; day set to 01 as the sources give the congress by month.
stops.campa: Sent as an anarchist delegate to the International Workers' Congress, he arrives to find that August Bebel has moved to exclude the anarchists from it altogether, and the motion carries. The German delegation then puts its own anarchists out of the hall by force, Landauer among them. The expelled hold a rump meeting elsewhere in the city, and he speaks there at length and with heat. He goes back to Berlin to the editorship of Der Sozialist and to an article that will put him in a Prussian prison by October.
suggested_refs: The 1893 International Socialist Workers' Congress at Zurich and Bebel's exclusion motion

stops.name: Sorau, the first cell
stops.date_confidence: October 1893 attested by month; day set to 01. The nine additional months for incitement are dated to December 1893 in the German article.
stops.campa: He is arrested in Berlin for an article in Der Sozialist urging disobedience of the law, and sent east to serve at Sorau in the Niederlausitz, a Prussian town that will be Polish Żary within his daughters' lifetimes. He is twenty-three. It is the first of the terms and there will be others, always for something printed: the state answers what he writes about it with time. Two months for the article. Then, in December, nine months more for incitement.
suggested_refs: The Prussian prison at Sorau, Niederlausitz, now Żary in Poland

stops.name: Berlin, marriage to Grete Leuschner
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, not resolved but adjudicated: the English article gives late 1891 or early 1892, the German article gives October 1894. The German date is followed here because it is the specific one and agrees with the household chronology. Day set to 01.
stops.campa: Out of prison and without money, he marries Margarethe Leuschner, a seamstress, called Grete. Two daughters follow, Charlotte and Marianne. It is a marriage between the editor of an outlawed paper and a woman who sews for a living, and it holds for something under five years. He is at this point a man with a police file, no income to speak of and no profession his family would recognise, carrying a conviction that the coming society will not be legislated into being but built alongside the old one, house by house.
suggested_refs: The Landauer-Leuschner household in Berlin, 1894-1899

stops.name: Kottbusser Straße 11, the cooperative called Befreiung
stops.date_confidence: 1 October 1895 attested to the day by the German article. The relaunch of Der Sozialist and the pamphlet Ein Weg zur Befreiung der Arbeiterklasse are dated to 1895 without months and are folded into this stop.
stops.campa: He relaunches Der Sozialist and publishes Ein Weg zur Befreiung der Arbeiterklasse, a plan for producer and consumer cooperatives that would feed and clothe their own members outside the market. On the first of October a shop opens on Kottbusser Straße under the name Befreiung, liberation. The theory is not a demand made of anyone. It is a proposal that socialists start living as socialists now, in the present tense, with their own bread and their own rent, and let the state find itself with nothing left to administer.
stops.quote: People do not live in the state. The state lives in the people.
stops.quote_source: 'Tucker's Revelation', in Revolution and Other Writings: A Political Reader, trans. and ed. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2010), p. 249
suggested_refs: The consumer cooperative Befreiung, Kottbusser Straße 11, Berlin, opened 1 October 1895
Gustav Landauer, Ein Weg zur Befreiung der Arbeiterklasse (1895)
sources: Wikiquote listing of Landauer, citing Kuhn

stops.name: London, the congress of 1896
stops.date_confidence: 1896 attested; the congress sat in late July and early August, and the day is set to 01 because the sources give only the year. The London pin is the city marker: no venue is named in the reachable material.
stops.campa: He crosses to London for the International Socialist Congress, where the anarchists are contested again and again largely excluded. He argues there for cooperatives among the peasantry, which the Marxists regard as the most backward class in Europe and which he regards as the one class still holding land. London is also where the exiles are: Kropotkin has been in England since the eighties, and the anarchist emigration keeps its presses and its quarrels going in a language Landauer reads easily. He goes home and keeps printing.
suggested_refs: The 1896 International Socialist Workers and Trade Union Congress, London

stops.name: Friedrichshagen, the colony on the Müggelsee
stops.date_confidence: October 1897 attested; day set to 01. The English chronology says he moved here 'separated from Grete', which is wrong: he moved with Grete and both daughters and lived here until May 1899. Coordinate corrected: one lens gave 52.4453 / 13.6247, which falls in the Müggelsee about 900 m south of the settlement.
stops.campa: In October he moves the household out to Friedrichshagen on the Müggelsee, the loose colony of naturalist writers, vegetarians, freethinkers and Nietzscheans strung along Berlin's eastern water. Grete comes, and the two girls, Charlotte and Marianne. The year before he had exposed a police spy, Commissar Bösel, in print, was arrested for it, and was acquitted. Out here the arguments are literary and the air is clean. Der Sozialist is dying. He stays eighteen months.
suggested_refs: The Friedrichshagener Dichterkreis on the Müggelsee, 1890s
sources: Friedrichshagen local research summarised at ptgustavlandauer

segments.name: Hedwig Lachmann, Tegel, and the Sermons of Meister Eckhart

stops.name: Berlin, a reading at Richard Dehmel's house
stops.date_confidence: 28 February 1899 attested by the German article on Hedwig Lachmann. Correction, stated rather than resolved: two chronologies place the meeting at the Neue Gemeinschaft in Schlachtensee, which the Hart brothers did not found until 1900. That attribution is an anachronism and is not followed. Dehmel's address in 1899 is not established in the reachable sources, so the stop sits on the Berlin city pin.
stops.campa: At a reading in the house of the poet Richard Dehmel, on the last day of February, he meets Hedwig Lachmann. She is thirty-three, a poet and a translator out of English and Hebrew, and her German Salome will be the text Richard Strauss sets to music. Landauer is twenty-eight and married. What passes between them at the reading is not recorded, but within ten weeks his marriage is over, and for the next nineteen years everything he writes will pass under her hand before it goes to a printer.
suggested_refs: Hedwig Lachmann's German Salome, the libretto text of Richard Strauss's opera

stops.name: Friedrichshagen, the letter Grete finds
stops.date_confidence: 4 May 1899 attested to the day by Friedrichshagen local research and the German article.
stops.campa: Grete finds a letter he has written to Hedwig Lachmann. On the fourth of May he leaves the flat by the lake. Charlotte and Marianne stay with their mother; the divorce will take four more years to come through, and he will pay for it out of an income he does not have. The colony that had taken him in as a writer with a household watches the household come apart inside it. He moves back into the city with a paper about to fold and a prosecution already running against him.
suggested_refs: The Landauer flat at Friedrichshagen, occupied October 1897 to May 1899
sources: Friedrichshagen local research summarised at ptgustavlandauer

stops.name: Tegel, six months and Meister Eckhart
stops.date_confidence: Correction: the six-month Ziethen sentence was served 18 August 1899 to 26 February 1900, not from March 1899 as two chronologies have it. Coordinate corrected: one lens gave 52.5896 / 13.2891, about 900 m northeast of the prison.
stops.campa: The case is the Ziethen affair: he had argued in print that a man convicted of murder was framed, and named the police commissioner who framed him. Libel. Six months in Tegel, from the eighteenth of August to the twenty-sixth of February. Inside he does the two pieces of work that make the rest of his thought possible. He turns the sermons of Meister Eckhart out of Middle High German into modern German. He also edits the manuscript of Mauthner's critique of language while the sentence runs.
suggested_refs: Gustav Landauer's modern German edition of Meister Eckhart's sermons, begun in Tegel
The Ziethen case and the libel prosecution of 1899

stops.name: Lützowplatz 14, a room on the third floor
stops.date_confidence: January 1901 attested by gustav-landauer.org's survey of his Berlin addresses; day set to 01. Correction: one chronology places this sublet after the England years, describing him as 'back from England'. It precedes them; the England stay begins in September 1901.
stops.campa: He takes a sublet room on the third floor of a house on Lützowplatz, one address in a run of temporary ones. Der Sozialist is dead in its second series. He is out of prison, out of his marriage, out of a paper, living on translation and reviewing, with Hedwig Lachmann keeping her own room elsewhere in the city because they cannot yet marry. The Eckhart manuscript is with him. So is the Mauthner. Neither has yet turned into the book that will make the two of them one argument.
suggested_refs: gustav-landauer.org, 'Wohnorte in Berlin', the survey of his Berlin addresses

stops.name: Bromley in Kent, in Kropotkin's orbit
stops.date_confidence: September 1901 to 1902 attested; day set to 01. Three corrections against one chronology: the stay is 1901-1902 and not 1899-1902, since he was in Tegel until February 1900; the place is Bromley in Kent, near Kropotkin, and not central London; and their daughter Gudula was not born in England but at Berlin-Hermsdorf after the return.
stops.campa: He and Hedwig Lachmann cross to England and settle at Bromley in Kent, where Peter Kropotkin has been living since the eighteen-eighties. Kropotkin's anarchist communism is built on mutual aid observed among animals and among Siberian villages, and Landauer will translate and popularise him in German. From England he writes to Martin Buber, the young Zionist he has begun corresponding with, the sentence that governs everything he will do in Munich eighteen years later.
stops.quote: A goal can only be reached if the means are in consonance with its essential nature. One will never attain non-violence through violence.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Martin Buber, 1901, cited in Maurice Friedman, Martin Buber's Life and Work, vol. I, p. 251
suggested_refs: Peter Kropotkin's house at Bromley, Kent
The Landauer-Buber correspondence, begun 1899-1900
sources: Wikiquote listing of Landauer, citing Friedman

stops.name: Schloßstraße 17, Hermsdorf: the first settled house
stops.date_confidence: June 1902 attested by gustav-landauer.org; day set to 01. Gudula's birth on 15 August 1902 at Berlin-Hermsdorf and Brigitte's in 1906 are folded into this stop; one chronology places Gudula's birth in England, which the genealogical record contradicts.
stops.campa: The couple come back from Kent and take a house on Schloßstraße in Hermsdorf, out among the pines north of Berlin, the first settled address either of them has had. Of all his Berlin addresses across nearly three decades, this is the only one carrying a plaque today. The suburb is chosen because it is cheap and quiet and the trains run into the city. On the fifteenth of August their daughter Gudula is born there, not in England as one chronology has it. A second girl, Brigitte, follows in 1906.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque at Schloßstraße 17, Berlin-Hermsdorf, the only Landauer plaque in Berlin

stops.name: Hermsdorf, Skepsis und Mystik
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day set to 01 to order the segment against the May marriage. No month of publication is given in the reachable sources.
stops.campa: He publishes Skepsis und Mystik: Versuche im Anschluss an Mauthners Sprachkritik, the book the prison cell had been assembling. The argument runs like this. Mauthner is right, language cannot reach the world, every word is the fossil of a dead perception; and therefore the sceptic who follows him honestly arrives not at nothing but at mysticism, at a direct standing in the world that no word can report on. The Eckhart he translated at Tegel is in it throughout, and Mauthner's name stands in the subtitle on the title page.
suggested_refs: Gustav Landauer, Skepsis und Mystik: Versuche im Anschluss an Mauthners Sprachkritik (1903)

stops.name: Berlin, the divorce and the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: May 1903 per the German articles on Landauer and Lachmann; day set to 01. One chronology gives only the year.
stops.campa: The divorce from Grete Leuschner comes through and he marries Hedwig Lachmann. She is not a wife in the domestic register the period expects: she translates Oscar Wilde, Edgar Allan Poe and Rabindranath Tagore, writes her own verse, and reads everything he writes before it leaves the house. They will have fifteen years. The household at Hermsdorf becomes known among their friends as a place where two people work in the same rooms at different desks, on different books, in more than one language.
suggested_refs: Hedwig Lachmann's translations of Wilde, Poe and Tagore, produced in the Hermsdorf household

stops.name: Hermsdorf, Die Revolution for Buber's series
stops.date_confidence: Volk und Land: Thirty Socialist Theses is dated January 1907; Die Revolution is dated 1907 without a month, and the two are folded into one stop dated 01 January. Buber's commission for the Rütten und Loening series Die Gesellschaft is dated from 1906.
stops.campa: Martin Buber, editing a social psychology series called Die Gesellschaft for the publisher Rütten und Loening, commissions Landauer alongside Simmel, Sombart and Tönnies. What Landauer hands him is Die Revolution, a short book that reads European history as an alternation: ages of organic community, in which people are bound to one another, and ages of topia, in which they are bound only to institutions. Revolution is the passage between the two. He has just published Volk und Land: Thirty Socialist Theses.
suggested_refs: Gustav Landauer, Die Revolution (1907), volume 13 of Buber's series Die Gesellschaft
Gustav Landauer, Volk und Land: Dreissig sozialistische Thesen (1907)
sources: martin_buber.journey.json, the Rütten und Loening commission

segments.name: The Socialist Bund and the Call to Socialism

stops.name: Berlin, the Twelve Articles
stops.date_confidence: June 1908 attested by month; day set to 01. The Bund had no headquarters and no single address; the Berlin city pin stands for a federation held together by post.
stops.campa: He founds the Sozialistischer Bund on twelve articles. It is not a party and will never contest an election. It is a federation of small groups, each meant to become a settlement that produces what it consumes and consumes what it produces, spreading by imitation rather than by capture of the state. Buber joins. So does Erich Mühsam, the Berlin bohemian poet who will stand beside him in Munich eleven years later. At its height the Bund runs to perhaps a thousand people in about twenty groups.
stops.quote: Anarchy is not a matter of the future; it is a matter of the present. It is not a matter of making demands; it is a matter of how one lives.
stops.quote_source: 'Anarchic Thoughts on Anarchism', in Revolution and Other Writings: A Political Reader, trans. and ed. Gabriel Kuhn (PM Press, 2010), p. 87
suggested_refs: The Twelve Articles of the Sozialistischer Bund, June 1908
sources: Wikiquote listing of Landauer, citing Kuhn

stops.name: Fellbacher Straße 26, Hermsdorf
stops.date_confidence: June 1908 attested by gustav-landauer.org; day set to 01. It shares a date with the founding of the Bund in the same month, and the two stops are ordered by sequence in the file rather than by day.
stops.campa: The family moves to a larger house on what is then Kaiserstraße in Hermsdorf: two daughters now, and a room for the Bund's correspondence. Landauer earns by translating, reviewing, and lecturing on literature to workers' associations, and by his wife's pen. There is no money in anarchism. There is a great deal of postage. The Bund is held together entirely by letters going out from this address, to groups in Zurich, Ascona, the Rhineland and Bavaria.
suggested_refs: gustav-landauer.org, 'Wohnorte in Berlin: 1902-1917'

stops.name: Monte Verità, above Ascona
stops.date_confidence: Summer 1908 attested by the German article; month set to July and day to 01 to order the segment. Correction: one chronology dates the Ascona visit to 1906, which is wrong. Coordinate taken byte-identical from the standing Monte Verità pin used elsewhere in this corpus, not from the two slightly different figures the lenses returned.
stops.campa: In the summer he climbs the hill above Ascona, where a colony of vegetarians, nudists, theosophists and refusers of every kind has been living in light and air huts since the turn of the century. They eat raw food, work the ground, wear as little as the season allows, and take orders from nobody. It is the twelve articles standing up in soil, and it is not his: he does not stay on the hill. Here he meets Margarethe Faas-Hardegger, the Swiss labour organiser. The Bund will keep a group at Ascona.
suggested_refs: The Monte Verità settlement above Ascona and its Lufthütten

stops.name: Berlin, Der Sozialist raised again
stops.date_confidence: January 1909 attested by month; day set to 01. The quoted article is dated 15 June 1910, a year and a half into this third series, and is attached here because the stop covers the paper's whole last life.
stops.campa: Der Sozialist comes back for its third and last life as the organ of the Sozialistischer Bund, printed twice a month in Berlin and edited by him alone out of the Hermsdorf house. Into it goes everything: the theses, the Eckhart, the reports from the groups, the polemics against the Social Democrats. On the fifteenth of June 1910 it carries an article on weak statesmen and a weaker people, and in that article one sentence anarchists have quoted ever since.
stops.quote: The state is a social relationship; a certain way of people relating to one another. It can be destroyed by creating new social relationships; i.e., by people relating to one another differently.
stops.quote_source: 'Schwache Staatsmänner, schwächeres Volk!', Der Sozialist, 15 June 1910, English text at theanarchistlibrary.org
suggested_refs: Der Sozialist, third series, 1909-1915, organ of the Sozialistischer Bund

stops.name: Hermsdorf, Aufruf zum Sozialismus
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; month and day set to 01. The confiscated pamphlet Die Abschaffung des Kriegs durch die Selbstbestimmung des Volks belongs to the same year and is folded into this stop. The quoted sentence is flagged: it is the widely circulated English rendering of the book's core thesis and could not be checked against a full-text edition, the one host consulted returning a 403.
stops.campa: He publishes Aufruf zum Sozialismus, the call to socialism, and it is a book-length attack on Karl Marx from the left. Historical materialism is a superstition; scientific socialism is not a science; the proletariat is not a messiah; and nothing whatever obliges the future to arrive. Socialism is something people build when they decide to, or it does not happen at all. In the same year the Berlin police confiscate his pamphlet on abolishing war through the self-determination of the people.
stops.quote: Socialism is possible at all times, if enough people want it.
stops.quote_source: Aufruf zum Sozialismus (1911), in the widely circulated English rendering; the exact wording is unverified against a full-text edition
suggested_refs: Gustav Landauer, Aufruf zum Sozialismus (1911), translated as For Socialism (Telos Press, 1978)
sources: archive.org listing, 'For socialism' by Gustav Landauer

segments.name: The War, the Volksheim, and Krumbach

stops.name: Oggenhausener Straße 2a, the last Berlin address
stops.date_confidence: June 1914 attested by gustav-landauer.org; day set to 01. The death of Der Sozialist in April 1915 is folded into this stop, since it happens at this address.
stops.campa: The last Berlin address, taken in June on what is then Tresckowstraße in Hermsdorf, a few streets from the Kaiserstraße house. He is forty-four. Two months after the move the war begins, and almost everyone he has argued with for twenty years goes over to it: the Social Democrats vote the credits, the Bund's groups empty into the army, the subscribers stop writing. He keeps Der Sozialist alive under censorship for eight more months, thinner with each number. The last issue appears in April 1915.
suggested_refs: The final issue of Der Sozialist, April 1915

stops.name: Max-Beer-Straße 5, the Jüdisches Volksheim
stops.date_confidence: 1916 attested by year; month and day set to 01. The quotation attached here is from his 1908 review of Buber's Baal Shem legends, not from 1916; it is placed on this stop because it states the position the Volksheim work follows from. The wording used is the Mendes-Flohr and Reinharz reading, which repairs a typo carried in two other printings.
stops.campa: In the Scheunenviertel, the crowded quarter behind the Alexanderplatz where Jews out of Galicia and Russia have settled, he presses for the opening of the Jüdisches Volksheim, a settlement house with a kindergarten, a library and evening classes. Buber's circle carries it. Landauer has been arguing since his review of Buber's Baal Shem legends that Judaism is not a confession a man may put down but a people he belongs to, and that a people without a state is the ordinary case rather than the tragic one.
stops.quote: Judaism is not an external contingency, but an inalienable inner property which transforms a number of individuals into a community.
stops.quote_source: Landauer's 1908 review of Martin Buber's Die Legende des Baalschem, as printed in Paul Mendes-Flohr and Jehuda Reinharz, eds., The Jew in the Modern World
suggested_refs: The Jüdisches Volksheim, Max-Beer-Straße 5, Berlin, opened 1916
sources: Mendes-Flohr and Reinharz, The Jew in the Modern World

stops.name: Berlin, the lectures with the war inside them
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction rather than attestation for the Aufbruchkreis material: the pacifist circle with Kurt Hiller and Ernst Joel and the veiled political content of the literary lectures are reported in summary form only, with no lecture text cited. The open letter to Woodrow Wilson is dated December 1916 and is also reported rather than reproduced. Day set to 01. The quotation is from a letter of 1914.
stops.campa: He moves in the pacifist circles the war has pushed underground, the Aufbruchkreis around Kurt Hiller and Ernst Joel, and lectures publicly on Goethe, Hölderlin and Shakespeare in halls where the police are listening, because a lecture on Hölderlin can say what a leaflet cannot. In December he writes an open letter to the President of the United States calling for a congress of the nations after the war. Nothing comes of it. He had already told Buber, in 1914, what he thought violence could produce.
stops.quote: Now it can become clear to man that freedom and peace of the nations can only come when as Jesus and his followers, and in our time above all Tolstoi advised, they choose to fully abstain from any violence.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Martin Buber, 1914, cited in Maurice Friedman, Martin Buber's Life and Work, vol. I, pp. 251-252
suggested_refs: Landauer's wartime lectures on Goethe, Hölderlin and Shakespeare
The open letter to Woodrow Wilson, December 1916
sources: Wikiquote listing of Landauer, citing Friedman

stops.name: Krumbach in Swabia, the flat at Hürben
stops.date_confidence: May 1917 attested; day set to 01. Correction of two loose statements in the lenses: the move is May and not 'early 1917', and Krumbach is not Hedwig Lachmann's birthplace. She was born at Stolp in Pomerania on 29 August 1865 and spent seven childhood years at Hürben, now part of Krumbach. His Berlin years run from 1889, about twenty-eight, not the 'roughly twenty-five' one lens gave.
stops.campa: Hedwig Lachmann's mother dies in February and leaves a flat standing empty at Hürben, now a part of Krumbach in Swabia. With the paper gone, the city hungry and the coal short, they take it. Krumbach is a market town in Bavarian Swabia, about as far from the Prussian police as a German anarchist can get without leaving Germany. Landauer leaves Berlin after twenty-eight years. Gudula and Brigitte come with him; Charlotte, the elder daughter of the first marriage, stays behind in Hermsdorf to mind the flat.
suggested_refs: The Lachmann family flat at Hürben, Krumbach

stops.name: Krumbach, the influenza
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Influenza takes her, and then pneumonia. She is fifty-two. Landauer is forty-seven, in a borrowed flat in a country town in the fourth winter of the war, with girls of fifteen and eleven, no income, and the woman who had read every page he wrote for nineteen years dead in the next room. He writes to friends that he does not know how to go on and does not particularly want to. Nine months later a letter comes from Munich asking him to help remake the souls of Bavaria.
suggested_refs: Hedwig Lachmann's grave at Krumbach

stops.name: Düsseldorf, the dramaturg's desk
stops.date_confidence: Gap acknowledged. The German summary gives only 'end of 1918' for the Düsseldorf dramaturgy, with no month, no contract and no production attached; the date here is set to October to order the segment before the Munich move of 15 November. It is the thinnest documented stop in the file.
stops.campa: Toward the end of the year he takes work as a dramaturg at the Schauspielhaus in Düsseldorf, a job in the theatre for a man who has been lecturing on Shakespeare for a decade and who needs to eat. It does not last. The record of these weeks is thin to the point of nothing: the summaries give the post and the city, no contract, no month, no production carrying his name. What he actually did at that desk is not known. In November the war ends and the King of Bavaria leaves Munich by motor car.
suggested_refs: The Schauspielhaus Düsseldorf under Louise Dumont and Gustav Lindemann

segments.name: Munich: Eisner's Letter and the Council Republic

stops.name: Munich, Eisner's letter
stops.date_confidence: Eisner's letter is dated 14 November 1918 and Landauer arrives in Munich on 15 November, both attested. Correction: one chronology gives October 1918, which is impossible, since Eisner had not yet taken power.
stops.campa: Kurt Eisner, a week after proclaiming the Bavarian republic in a city whose king had simply driven away, writes to Landauer and asks him to come and work on the transformation of souls. Landauer goes the next day. He arrives in a Munich where the theatres, the barracks, the ministries and the newspapers are all in the hands of men who did not have them a fortnight ago, and where the revolution is being conducted by a drama critic. He is forty-eight years old and has been waiting for this since 1892.
stops.quote: dass Sie durch Vortragstätigkeit an der Umbildung der Seelen mitwirken
stops.quote_source: Kurt Eisner to Gustav Landauer, letter of 14 November 1918
suggested_refs: Eisner's letter of invitation, 14 November 1918
sources: literaturportal-bayern.de, '15. November 1918: Ernst Toller und Gustav Landauer treffen in München ein'

stops.name: Munich, the Revolutionary Workers' Council
stops.date_confidence: Mid-November 1918 attested: he entered the Revolutionärer Arbeiterrat and the Zentralrat immediately on arriving on 15 November. The day is set to 16 only to order this stop after the arrival. Correction: one chronology dates the council membership to December, a month late.
stops.campa: He enters the Revolutionärer Arbeiterrat and the Zentralrat at once, and argues in both for what he has argued in print since 1908: that the councils themselves are the government, that a parliament elected across the whole of Bavaria will hand the revolution straight back to the parties that voted the war credits, and that the elections should therefore be postponed. He loses the argument. The Landtag elections are held in January and Eisner's party takes three seats out of a hundred and eighty.
suggested_refs: The Revolutionärer Arbeiterrat and the Zentralrat of the Bavarian revolution, November 1918

stops.name: Munich, the day Eisner is shot
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the Munich city pin is used, as the assassination site on the Promenadestraße is not separately given in the lenses
stops.campa: On his way to the Landtag to hand in his resignation, Kurt Eisner is shot in the back by Anton Graf von Arco auf Valley. Munich goes over into three months of improvisation, gunfire and committees, with no government anyone recognises and several claiming to be it. For Landauer the date carries a second weight: Hedwig Lachmann had died on the twenty-first of February the year before, to the day. Within seven weeks he will hold office in Bavaria. Within ten he will be dead.
suggested_refs: The assassination of Kurt Eisner, Munich, 21 February 1919

stops.name: Wittelsbacher Palais, Beauftragter für Volksaufklärung
stops.date_confidence: 7 April 1919 attested for the proclamation; the delegates had met at the Wittelsbacher Palais on 5 April and resolved on it there. Coordinate corrected: one lens gave 48.1436 / 11.5799, about 600 m from the palace at Brienner Straße 20. The Whitman line is a reported summary of his school policy, not a verified verbatim utterance.
stops.campa: Delegates meeting in the Wittelsbacher Palais on Brienner Straße resolve on a council republic, and it is proclaimed on the seventh. Landauer is made Beauftragter für Volksaufklärung, commissioner for enlightenment and public instruction, with the schools, the university and the theatres of Bavaria in his charge. He drafts at speed: history teaching remade, religious instruction made voluntary, the university thrown open, professors elected by their students. Erich Mühsam sits in the same government. It lasts six days.
stops.quote: Every Bavarian child at the age of 10 is going to know Walt Whitman by heart.
stops.quote_source: Reported summary of his programme as commissar for enlightenment, quoted in the libcom.org biographical entry; given there as paraphrase rather than a cited document
suggested_refs: The Wittelsbacher Palais, Brienner Straße 20, seat of the first Bavarian Räterepublik
Landauer's school and university decrees, April 1919

stops.name: Munich, the resignation
stops.date_confidence: 16 April 1919 attested by the German article; the Communist takeover of the council republic on 13 April is also attested
stops.campa: The Communists take the council republic on the thirteenth and run it as a dictatorship of the proletariat, with a Red Army and hostages. Landauer, who has spent twenty years writing that the means and the end are the same substance, will not serve it. On the sixteenth he resigns every office he holds and writes that the whole thing has been ruined. He does not leave Munich. He has nowhere to go and two daughters in Krumbach, and he stays in a city the Freikorps are already marching on.
suggested_refs: Landauer's letter of resignation, 16 April 1919

stops.name: Großhadern, the house at the western edge
stops.date_confidence: 1 May 1919 attested. Two accounts of the same arrest: the German article names a house in Großhadern, and Eugene Lunn names the house of Kurt Eisner's widow. They are taken as the same house here, though no source states the identification outright.
stops.campa: Government troops and Freikorps enter Munich at the end of April and take it street by street, shooting prisoners as they go. Landauer has gone to ground in Großhadern at the western edge of the city, in the house of Kurt Eisner's widow. Soldiers find him there on the first of May. He is a name on a list of the council republic's ministers, and the list is being worked through in the order it was printed. He is forty-nine years old, and he does not resist the arrest.
suggested_refs: Eugene Lunn, Prophet of Community: The Romantic Socialism of Gustav Landauer (1973), on the arrest and the days that follow
sources: Eugene Lunn, Prophet of Community, p. 338

stops.name: Starnberg, the night under guard
stops.date_confidence: attested; shares the day with the arrest at Großhadern and is ordered after it by sequence in the file
stops.campa: He is driven south to Starnberg on the lake and held there overnight under guard. In the morning they put him back in a vehicle for Munich, for the prison at Stadelheim on the far side of the city. Twenty-five kilometres of Bavarian lake country lie between the arrest and the courtyard. Somebody afterward wrote down where the vehicle had stopped for the night; nobody wrote down anything else. Whether he was questioned, whether he slept, whether anyone there spoke to him at all, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The transport chain of 1-2 May 1919: Großhadern, Starnberg, Stadelheim
sources: Eugene Lunn, Prophet of Community, p. 338

stops.name: Stadelheim, the passage
stops.date_confidence: 2 May 1919 attested. Correction of placement: the quoted words are often printed as spoken at the arrest on 1 May, but Lunn's sequence puts them in the passage at Stadelheim on the morning of the second, minutes before the killing. Coordinate corrected: two lenses gave 48.0836 / 11.5814 and 48.0781 / 11.6069, up to 2.6 km from the prison at Stadelheimer Straße 12.
stops.campa: He is brought into Stadelheim on the morning of the second and driven along a passage toward the courtyard with rifle butts. Soldiers and officers who have spent a week fighting in a city they were told was held by Russians and Jews close in around him. An eyewitness account, given afterward to Ernst Toller, has him turning to them as they strike. He is reported to have said also, that same morning, that death was coming now and a man should hold his head up.
stops.quote: I've not betrayed you. You don't know yourselves how terribly you've been betrayed
stops.quote_source: Eyewitness account given to Ernst Toller, printed in Toller's I Was a German and quoted in Eugene Lunn, Prophet of Community, p. 338
suggested_refs: Ernst Toller, Eine Jugend in Deutschland (I Was a German), for the eyewitness account of the killing
sources: Eugene Lunn, Prophet of Community, p. 338

stops.name: Stadelheim, the courtyard
stops.date_confidence: 2 May 1919 attested; shares the day with the previous stop and follows it by sequence. The English wording of the last words is uncertain: a fuller and a shorter form both circulate, and the German is given as 'Erschlagt mich doch. Daß ihr Menschen seid.'
stops.campa: In the courtyard they beat him with rifle butts and boots and then shoot him. The wounds recorded afterward are to the left eye socket, the right forehead and the left chest. Among the men is Eugen Digele, who takes Landauer's watch off the body. Digele is tried in March 1920 and given five weeks, for assault and for receiving stolen goods; nobody is ever tried for the killing. Franz Freiherr von Gagern is court-martialled in September 1919 over the death and fined five hundred marks.
stops.quote: Kill me then! To think that you are human!
stops.quote_source: Reported last words to the Freikorps soldiers, Stadelheim, 2 May 1919; wording uncertain, the German circulating as 'Erschlagt mich doch. Daß ihr Menschen seid.'
suggested_refs: The courtyard of the Justizvollzugsanstalt München, Stadelheimer Straße 12
The March 1920 trial of Eugen Digele

stops.name: Nordfriedhof, the urn hall
stops.date_confidence: The urn stands in the Nordfriedhof urn hall from 1919 to 1923, attested as a span; month and day are set to order the segment, not from a record of the deposit.
stops.campa: The body is cremated and the urn set in the urn hall of the Nordfriedhof, where it stands for four years. There is no funeral the authorities will permit and no grave to put it in: the Bavarian government has only just finished shooting the people who would have carried it. His daughters are in Krumbach. His friends are in prison, Mühsam among them, sentenced to fifteen years in a fortress. The urn waits on a shelf in a municipal building among the urns of ordinary Munich dead.
suggested_refs: The urn hall of the Munich Nordfriedhof

stops.name: Waldfriedhof, the obelisk of the Freie Arbeiter-Union
stops.date_confidence: The urn is moved to the Waldfriedhof in 1923 and the obelisk raised in May 1925, both attested; day set to 01. Coordinate corrected: two lenses gave 48.12 / 11.49 and 48.1103 / 11.4933, both north of the cemetery on Fürstenrieder Straße in Hadern.
stops.campa: In 1923 the urn is moved out to the Waldfriedhof at Hadern, a cemetery laid out among pines, and in May 1925 the anarcho-syndicalists of the Freie Arbeiter-Union Deutschlands raise a five metre obelisk over it. The inscription they choose is not a battle cry. It is a passage of Landauer's own about the kind of sacrifice that would actually be required, and it says very nearly the opposite of what a monument over a murdered revolutionary is expected to say. Cut into the stone, six years after the courtyard, are his own words:
stops.quote: Further sacrifices are required. However, they will be sacrifices of a different kind: not heroic, but quiet and unimposing; examples of righteousness in everyday life.
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the FAUD obelisk over Landauer's grave, Waldfriedhof, Munich, 1925, as given by PM Press
suggested_refs: The 1925 FAUD obelisk at the Munich Waldfriedhof
sources: PM Press, 'Gustav Landauer Monument in Munich to be Reerected' (2019)

stops.name: Waldfriedhof, the monument pulled down
stops.date_confidence: June 1933 attested; day set to 01. Correction: one lens says the destruction came 'weeks after taking power', which is wrong. Power was seized on 30 January 1933 and the obelisk came down about five months later.
stops.campa: The Munich city council resolves to remove the grave monuments of Marxist revolutionaries, and in June the obelisk comes down, five months after the seizure of power rather than in the first weeks of it. The urn is dug up and handed over to the Jewish community of Munich, which is then sent the bill for the exhumation. The community pays it. The stone is broken up, the plot in the pines is levelled, and what is left at the Waldfriedhof is ground with nothing standing on it.
suggested_refs: The 1933 Munich city council decision on the grave monuments of 'Marxist revolutionaries'
Munich Gedenkbuch and nsdoku.de records of the 1933 grave destructions

stops.name: Neuer Israelitischer Friedhof, beside Kurt Eisner
stops.date_confidence: The reburial with Eisner follows the 1933 exhumation; the separate grave dates to 1946, on his daughter Gudula's initiative, with no month recorded, so month and day are set to 01. Coordinate: two lenses gave 48.1073 / 11.5442, some 9 km off in Sendling, and 48.1821 / 11.6008; the figure used here is the Garchinger Straße one. One lens says Eisner and Landauer died six weeks apart, which is wrong: 21 February to 2 May 1919 is ten weeks.
stops.campa: Martin Buber had gathered his letters and printed them in two volumes in 1929, four years before the obelisk came down; the paper outlasted the granite. The remains themselves come at last to the new Jewish cemetery on Garchinger Straße, into a double grave with Kurt Eisner, the two of them ten weeks apart in the spring of 1919 and finally under one stone. In 1946, on the initiative of his daughter Gudula, a separate grave is arranged for him there.
stops.quote: Landauer fell like a prophet and a martyr of the human community to come.
stops.quote_source: Martin Buber, tribute written after Landauer's murder, quoted in the libcom.org biographical entry
suggested_refs: Martin Buber, ed., Gustav Landauer: sein Lebensgang in Briefen, 2 vols. (1929)
The Eisner and Landauer graves, Neuer Israelitischer Friedhof, Garchinger Straße 37, Munich

stops.name: Waldfriedhof, the obelisk raised again
stops.date_confidence: Gap acknowledged. PM Press's 2019 article frames the unveiling as 2017 but gives no date, and no independent confirmation was reachable, so month and day are set to 01. The initiative is dated to early 2015 and the unanimous council vote to November 2015; the limited competition was won in spring 2016 by Markus Knittel of F. X. Rauch Grabmale. No source calls Peter Kühn a member of a 'Martin Buber Society', and that description is dropped.
stops.campa: An initiative begun in 2015 by Peter Kühn and the historian Siegbert Wolf, taken up by the city councillor Thomas Ranft, brings the destroyed memorial back before the council, which votes unanimously for restoration in November of that year. A limited competition follows and is won in the spring of 2016 by Markus Knittel. The new monument goes up at the Waldfriedhof. Eighty-four years after the obelisk was broken, the plot in the pines has a stone on it again.
suggested_refs: The re-erected Landauer memorial at the Munich Waldfriedhof
raete-muenchen.de and anarchismus.at on the restoration campaign
sources: PM Press, 'Gustav Landauer Monument in Munich to be Reerected' (2019)
